lessons.loto-purpose-overview:
**Purpose and Overview of Lockout/Tagout**

Lockout/tagout (LOTO) is the process of isolating hazardous energy before employees perform servicing, maintenance, cleaning, adjusting, or repair on powered equipment. OSHA 1910.147, the Control of Hazardous Energy standard, establishes the requirements. The purpose is to prevent unexpected startup, energization, or release of stored energy that could injure workers. Tags provide information and warning but do not physically prevent energization — locks provide the physical barrier. Energy control must be verified before work begins.
lessons.hazardous-energy-types:
**Types of Hazardous Energy**

Equipment can contain multiple forms of hazardous energy: electrical (stored in capacitors or wiring), hydraulic (pressure in lines or cylinders), pneumatic (compressed air), mechanical (springs under tension, rotating parts with inertia), thermal (steam, heat), and gravitational (elevated loads or parts). Each energy source must be identified in the written energy control procedure and isolated or controlled before work begins. Assumptions about which energy sources are present can lead to serious injuries.
lessons.authorized-affected-employees:
**Authorized and Affected Employees**

An authorized employee is one who is trained and authorized to apply lockout/tagout devices to control hazardous energy before service or maintenance work. An affected employee is one whose job requires operating or using equipment that is being serviced, or who works in an area where LOTO is being performed. Affected employees must be trained to recognize lockout/tagout devices and must never attempt to restart or energize locked or tagged equipment. Only the authorized employee who applied a lockout device normally removes it.
lessons.loto-procedures:
**LOTO Procedures: Isolation and Verification**

Written energy control procedures must be followed for each piece of equipment. The sequence includes: notify affected employees, shut down the equipment using normal stopping procedure, isolate all energy sources, apply lockout/tagout devices to each energy isolating device, control or release stored energy, and verify that the equipment will not operate. If arc flash hazards are present, electrical safety procedures must also be followed. When maintenance is complete and equipment is ready for return to service, all tools must be cleared, employees moved out of the danger zone, and affected employees notified before locks are removed.
lessons.stored-energy-control:
**Stored Energy Control**

After the main power source is shut off, hazardous energy can still remain in equipment. Stored energy examples include: residual hydraulic pressure in lines after a pump is shut down, springs under compression or tension, gravity-loaded components (raised lifts, suspended loads), capacitor charge in electrical systems, steam trapped in pipes, and rotating equipment coasting to a stop. Each form of stored energy must be relieved, restrained, blocked, bled, or otherwise controlled before work begins. Failure to address stored energy is a leading cause of lockout/tagout injuries.
lessons.group-loto:
**Group Lockout and Special Situations**

When multiple authorized employees work on the same equipment, group lockout must ensure that every employee is personally protected. Each authorized employee must apply their own personal lock to a hasp or group lockout device. One shared lock or tag is not sufficient — everyone must have personal protection. Complex equipment with multiple energy sources requires coordination, and shift changes require transition of lockout protection. When contractors perform work on-site, the host employer and contractor must coordinate LOTO procedures and exchange information about energy control requirements.
lessons.return-to-service:
**Returning Equipment to Service**

Before locked-out equipment is returned to normal service, a specific sequence must be followed: ensure all tools, spare parts, and nonessential materials have been removed; confirm the equipment has been reassembled correctly; ensure all employees are safely positioned away from the danger zone; notify all affected employees that lockout is being removed and equipment is about to be restarted; then remove lockout devices in accordance with the energy control procedure and re-energize. A temporary restart during testing requires the same careful steps as a full release, followed by re-application of lockout/tagout before work resumes.

1.questionText: Lockout/tagout procedures are used primarily to:

options.text: Speed up equipment maintenance cycles
Protect workers from unexpected energization or release of hazardous energy during service
Lower equipment repair costs
Record equipment inventory

2.questionText: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 is the standard that governs:

options.text: Hazard communication and chemical labeling
Control of hazardous energy — lockout/tagout
Emergency action plans
Respiratory protection

3.questionText: After the main power source for a piece of equipment is turned off, stored energy such as hydraulic pressure or spring tension may still be present.

options.text: True
False

options.text: Authorized employee
Affected employee
Entry supervisor
Safety officer

options.text: Inform the plant manager that work is starting
Verify that the equipment cannot be energized or started

6.questionText: A tagout device alone physically locks out equipment and prevents it from being energized.

options.text: True
False

7.questionText: A lockout device should be removed by:

options.text: The shift supervisor at the end of the maintenance window
Any employee who is ready to restart the machine
The authorized employee who originally applied it
Any available maintenance technician

options.text: Share a single lock attached by the crew leader
Apply their own personal lock to ensure individual protection
Verify only that the supervisor's lock is in place

9.questionText: A hydraulic press has been powered down, but pressure gauges still show elevated pressure in the lines. Before maintenance begins, the worker must:

options.text: Begin work since the motor is no longer running
Relieve, bleed, or block the residual hydraulic pressure
Remove tags but leave the lockout in place

10.questionText: Before releasing a lockout and returning equipment to service, which of the following is required?

options.text: Remove all tools and nonessential materials from the equipment
Ensure employees are clear of the danger zone
Notify affected employees that equipment is being restarted

options.text: Disregard the label since lockout procedures are already being followed
Remove the label to avoid confusion during maintenance
Follow the facility's electrical safety procedures and consult a supervisor if unsure

options.text: Leave the locks off after testing and continue work
Complete the release procedure for testing, then fully reapply lockout/tagout before resuming maintenance
Have an affected employee hold the start button during the test

Electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, mechanical, thermal, and gravitational energy

options.text: True
